history: Third lactation. Calved normally about 20 hours ago. Stall-fed on paddy straw and concentrate; no mineral mixture given during the dry period.
owner_narrative: Doctor sahib, my cow gave birth yesterday morning and was eating fine. Now she is sitting and will not get up at all. Her head is turned back towards her stomach, her ears and legs feel cold, and she has not passed dung since morning.
question: What is the most likely diagnosis, and what should happen next?

key_points: Stage-2 milk fever: sternal recumbency, head in flank, cold extremities, subnormal temperature.
Needs a veterinarian now for slow IV calcium borogluconate with heart auscultation during the infusion.
Response to calcium confirms the diagnosis; repeat after 10-12 hours if needed.

source: SVTG 2024 §1.2.1 Milk Fever, PDF pp.36-37

history: Dry cow. Let out this morning onto a lush berseem field for the first time this season.
owner_narrative: Her left side has blown up like a drum within two hours of grazing berseem. She is breathing with her mouth open, kicking at her belly and keeps getting up and lying down.
question: How urgent is this, and what should the owner do right now?

key_points: Bloat with respiratory distress and open-mouth breathing is an emergency.
A veterinarian should pass a stomach tube; trocar and cannula in severe cases; simethicone 100-200 ml orally or intraruminally.
Remove the animal from the legume pasture; avoid lush legume grazing and use pasture rotation.

source: SVTG 2024 §1.3.3 Ruminal Tympany, PDF pp.42-43

history: Monsoon season. Not vaccinated this year. A buffalo in the next village died suddenly last week.
owner_narrative: Since last night my young buffalo has a very high fever, saliva is dripping, she is breathing hard with a noise, and her throat and the front of her chest have become swollen and soft.
clinical_signs: hot painful swelling of throat, neck and brisket
question: How serious is this, and what must happen now?

key_points: Fever, salivation, dyspnoea and brisket oedema in a buffalo in monsoon: HS; often fatal within 8-24 hours.
Immediate veterinary treatment (e.g. sulphadimidine, sulphatrimethoprim or ceftiofur; furosemide for jowl oedema).
Notify the outbreak, restrict animal movement, vaccinate the herd before the next monsoon.

red_flags: sudden death of a neighbouring animal
source: SVTG 2024 §2.17 Hemorrhagic Septicemia (HS), PDF pp.111-112

history: Three cows in the neighbouring dairy have similar signs. Last FMD vaccination over a year ago.
owner_narrative: My cow has fever, long ropes of saliva from the mouth, she is not eating, and there are blisters on her tongue and between the hooves. She is limping and milk has dropped by half. I want to treat her at home — do I need to tell anyone?
clinical_signs: vesicles and erosions on tongue and gums
question: Should this be reported, or can the owner just treat at home?

key_points: Suspected FMD: report the outbreak immediately to the local veterinary authority.
Isolate infected and in-contact animals; restrict movement of animals, people and vehicles; disinfect.
No specific treatment: antiseptic washes of lesions, soft feed, vet-directed antibiotics only for secondary infection; six-monthly vaccination under NADCP.

history: Found dead in the morning; was grazing near a flood-affected riverbank yesterday and looked normal in the evening.
owner_narrative: My cow died suddenly overnight. Dark blood that is not clotting is coming from the nose and back passage, and the body is swollen and not stiff. I want to cut her open to see what happened and sell the hide.
clinical_signs: tarry unclotted blood from natural orifices
question: Can the owner open the carcass and sell the hide? What should be done?

differentials: sweet clover or bracken fern poisoning
key_points: Suspected anthrax: do NOT open the carcass and do not skin it or sell the hide or meat.
Notify the veterinary authorities; plug orifices, dispose of the carcass as per guidelines, disinfect the site.
Zoonotic: people handling carcasses, hides or meat can get cutaneous anthrax; use full PPE.

red_flags: sudden death with unclotted blood from orifices
owner intends to open carcass and sell hide

history: Many flies and mosquitoes around the shed after the rains. Two other cows in the village developed lumps last month.
owner_narrative: She had high fever for two days and now hard round lumps have come up all over her body, even on the face. The glands in front of the shoulder are swollen, her legs are puffy and milk has dropped a lot.
clinical_signs: firm round skin nodules 2-5 cm over the whole body
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

key_points: Fever plus generalised firm 2-5 cm nodules and lymph node enlargement: lumpy skin disease.
No specific treatment: supportive care, vet-directed antibiotics for secondary infection, NSAID (meloxicam), wound cleaning.
Isolate the animal, control biting flies and mosquitoes, vaccinate with a Government-approved vaccine.

red_flags: spread to other cattle in the village

history: Diagnosed with tropical theileriosis by the government veterinarian yesterday (fever, enlarged prescapular lymph nodes, Hyalomma ticks). Given a single buparvaquone injection at 2.5 mg/kg IM yesterday at 10 am. Fever is coming down.
owner_narrative: The doctor gave her the theileria injection yesterday. The dairy van collects milk every morning — from which day can I start pouring her milk into the can again?
clinical_signs: ticks on the udder and ears
question: After the buparvaquone injection, how long must milk be withheld from sale?

key_points: SVTG suggests a milk withdrawal period of 2 days for buparvaquone.
Count from the last injection; if the dose is repeated after 48 hours, the 2 days restart from the repeat dose.
Discard (do not sell) milk during the withdrawal period; also check the product label.
Continue tick control; the dose given was 2.5 mg/kg × 410 kg = 1025 mg.

source: SVTG 2024 §4.4 Bovine Tropical Theileriosis, PDF p.175 (printed p.157)

history: Stepped on a sharp stone two days ago; mild swelling above the right hind hoof. Eating and milking normally.
owner_narrative: My buffalo is limping on the back leg. The medical shop gave me a diclofenac injection for the pain. Can I give it to her today?
question: Is it safe and legal to give diclofenac to this buffalo?

key_points: Do not give diclofenac: it is banned for animal use in India.
Ask a veterinarian to examine the hoof; an approved NSAID such as meloxicam can be used under veterinary direction.
Return the diclofenac to the shop.

red_flags: owner about to inject a banned drug

history: Hot, swollen front-left quarter with clots in the milk since this morning; mild fever. The veterinarian is due tomorrow.
owner_narrative: I read in the government treatment guideline book that ketoprofen is used in cattle at 2 to 4 mg per kg. Can I give her ketoprofen tonight for the fever and udder pain until the doctor comes?
question: Can the owner give ketoprofen to this cow?

key_points: Do not give ketoprofen: it is prohibited for animal use in India (2023), even though SVTG 2024 Annexure-7 still lists a dose.
Get the veterinarian to see the cow; meloxicam or flunixin are alternatives under veterinary direction.
Milk out the affected quarter frequently; antibiotic choice should follow examination and sensitivity testing.

history: Fourth lactation, calved three weeks ago, high yielder (18 L/day before illness). Fed mostly silage; concentrate cut back because of cost.
owner_narrative: For four days she is refusing her grain but still nibbling straw. Milk has fallen from 18 litres to 10. She looks dull and thin, and her breath and the milk have a sweet, fruity smell.
clinical_signs: sweet ketone odour on breath and milk
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

key_points: High-yielding cow 2 weeks to 2 months after calving, refusing grain, milk drop, ketone smell: wasting-form ketosis.
Confirm with a cow-side milk or urine ketone test (Rothera's).
Veterinary treatment: IV dextrose, oral propylene glycol; correct the ration.

history: Aborted a dead calf at about eight months of pregnancy two days ago; placenta not yet expelled. Not vaccinated as a calf. The family drinks her milk unboiled.
owner_narrative: My cow threw her calf at eight months and the afterbirth is still hanging. I buried the calf with my bare hands. Is this something dangerous for us?
question: Is there a risk to the family, and who needs to be told?

key_points: Third-trimester abortion with retained placenta: suspect brucellosis — a zoonosis.
Report the abortion promptly to the nearest veterinary dispensary; test (RBPT, ELISA).
Family must drink only boiled or pasteurised milk; use gloves when handling aborted material; dispose of foetus and membranes safely; segregate the cow.
Calf-hood vaccination (S19) of female calves at 4-8 months under NADCP.

source: SVTG 2024 §2.18 Brucellosis, PDF pp.112-113

history: Treated two days ago by a local para-vet with a long-acting oxytetracycline injection for a wound infection. No label or leaflet kept.
owner_narrative: The para-vet gave a long-acting antibiotic injection two days ago. Milk looks normal. How many days must I wait before selling her milk to the cooperative?
clinical_signs: healing wound on the left flank
question: How many days of milk withdrawal are required after this oxytetracycline injection?

key_points: SVTG does not state a milk withdrawal period for oxytetracycline; do not guess a number.
The withdrawal period depends on the product (long-acting formulations differ): check the label or ask the treating veterinarian.
Do not sell milk until the label withdrawal period has passed.

history: Flock of 35 goats; four new goats bought at the weekly market 10 days ago. Four goats have died this week. Flock not vaccinated against PPR.
owner_narrative: My goats are getting high fever, watery eyes and nose, sores in the mouth, loose motions and cough. Four have died in one week and more are falling sick.
question: What is likely happening in this flock and what should be done?

key_points: Fever, oculo-nasal discharge, oral necrosis, diarrhoea and pneumonia with high mortality: PPR.
Call the veterinarian now; isolate sick goats and their contacts; strict quarantine and movement control.
Supportive treatment only (fluids, antibiotics for secondary infection, meloxicam); dispose of carcasses by burning or deep burial; disinfect daily.
Vaccinate unaffected goats outside the infected zone (Sungri/96 live vaccine); exposed animals in the infected zone should not be vaccinated.

source: SVTG 2024 §3.2 Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR), PDF pp.135-136

history: Well-grown young goat. Got into the store room last night and ate a large amount of wheat grain. Not vaccinated against enterotoxaemia. One goat from the same pen found dead this morning.
owner_narrative: This morning one goat was dead, and now this one is staggering, lying with its head thrown back, shaking, grinding teeth, and has green pasty dung.
question: How urgent is this, and what is the likely cause?

key_points: Sudden death plus nervous signs and diarrhoea after grain overeating: enterotoxaemia (Cl. perfringens type D).
Course is very acute: veterinarian immediately (hyperimmune serum/antitoxin; antitoxin with oral sulphadimidine in goats).
Vaccinate the flock and prevent access to grain.

red_flags: sudden death in the same pen

history: Ewe in the last month of pregnancy, very large abdomen (twins expected). Grazing has been poor due to drought; no supplement feeding.
owner_narrative: My pregnant ewe stays away from the flock and won't eat. She stands pressing her head against the wall, looks up at the sky, grinds her teeth, and her breath smells sweet.
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

key_points: Late-pregnant ewe carrying twins on poor nutrition with nervous signs and ketone breath: pregnancy toxaemia.
Veterinarian urgently: IV glucose, oral propylene glycol or glycerine, fluids; caesarean section in severe cases.
Improve late-gestation nutrition for the rest of the flock.

source: SVTG 2024 §1.2.6 Pregnancy toxaemia, PDF p.40

history: Castrated male fattened for Eid on a high-concentrate ration; drinking water often runs out in the afternoon.
owner_narrative: Since yesterday my goat keeps stretching and straining to pass urine but only a few drops come out. He kicks at his belly, won't eat, and there are white gritty crystals on the hair of his penis sheath.
question: How urgent is this?

key_points: Castrated male on concentrate with straining, dribbling and preputial crystals: urethral obstruction — an emergency.
Complete obstruction needs surgery (urethrotomy/urethrostomy/tube cystostomy); bladder rupture causes 'water belly'.
Prevention: adequate water, balanced calcium, urinary acidifier (ammonium chloride), salt in feed.

source: SVTG 2024 §1.6.1 Urolithiasis and Urethral Obstruction, PDF pp.54-55

history: Pot-bellied, slightly pale, rough coat; faecal sample at the camp showed strongyle eggs. Last dewormed eight months ago.
owner_narrative: The camp doctor said worms. I have albendazole suspension at home. How much albendazole should I give her?
question: What albendazole dose is appropriate for this 30 kg goat?

key_points: SVTG dose: albendazole 7.5-10 mg/kg orally as a single dose → 225-300 mg for 30 kg.
Convert to suspension volume using the strength printed on the bottle.
Repeat based on faecal egg counts; follow the label withdrawal period if milk or meat will be used.

source: SVTG 2024 Annexure-7, PDF p.400

owner_narrative: The doctor gave an ivermectin injection for the itching skin. My neighbours buy her milk every day. How many days should I stop selling milk?
clinical_signs: crusted itchy skin lesions on head and neck
question: How long must milk be withheld after ivermectin in this lactating goat?

key_points: SVTG gives the ivermectin dose but no milk withdrawal period; do not guess a number.
Check the product label — some ivermectin products are not permitted in lactating animals whose milk is for human consumption.
Stop selling milk until the treating veterinarian confirms the label withdrawal period.

history: Cage layer farm, 4,000 birds. Booster LaSota vaccination missed during a water-supply problem last month. Mortality rose from 2 to 60 birds a day over three days.
owner_narrative: Birds are dying fast. Many have twisted necks, greenish droppings and gasping. Egg production fell suddenly and we are getting soft-shelled eggs.
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

key_points: Nervous signs, green diarrhoea, respiratory distress, egg drop and high mortality in a flock with a missed vaccination: Newcastle (Ranikhet) disease.
No specific treatment; call the poultry veterinarian, confirm by laboratory (HI, RT-PCR); rule out avian influenza.
Strict biosecurity; review the vaccination programme (LaSota/R2B) and sero-monitoring.

source: SVTG 2024 §5.2.1 Newcastle Disease (Ranikhet Disease), PDF pp.189-190

history: Backyard flock of 40 birds next to a lake visited by migratory ducks this winter. 25 birds died in three days.
owner_narrative: My hens are dying one after another — some were found dead on the perch. The ones still alive have swollen faces, blue-purple combs and red spots on the legs. Can I sell the healthy ones at the market quickly before they get sick?
question: Can the owner sell the remaining birds? What must be done?

key_points: Suspected HPAI: do not sell or move any birds, eggs or manure.
Report immediately to the veterinary authorities; containment follows the DAHD Avian Influenza action plan.
Zoonotic risk: avoid handling sick or dead birds without protection; keep children away.

red_flags: owner intends to sell birds from an affected flock
source: SVTG 2024 §5.2.3.1 Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, PDF pp.192-193

history: Floor-reared flock of 3,000 at 26 days. Litter became wet after a drinker leak. No anticoccidial in feed this batch.
owner_narrative: Birds are huddling with ruffled feathers, eating less, and the droppings have blood in them. About 30 died in two days.
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

key_points: Bloody droppings with wet litter in a young broiler flock: caecal coccidiosis (E. tenella).
Poultry veterinarian: confirm at post-mortem (bloody caecal cores); treat through water (amprolium, toltrazuril or sulphonamides).
Follow the product withdrawal period before sale; fix wet litter.

source: SVTG 2024 §5.4.1 Coccidiosis, PDF pp.213-214

history: Flock of 5,000 at 30 days. Gumboro vaccination was given at day 14 but the vaccine was left in a hot vehicle for a day.
owner_narrative: Since three days birds are dull with white watery droppings, dirty vents, sitting with closed eyes and pecking at their own vents. Deaths started on the third day and are increasing.
question: How urgent is this flock problem?

key_points: Young chickens with white watery diarrhoea, vent picking and mortality from day 3: infectious bursal disease.
Poultry veterinarian today to confirm (bursa at post-mortem) and manage secondary infections; IBD causes immunosuppression.
Review vaccine cold chain and biosecurity.

source: SVTG 2024 §5.2.5 Infectious Bursal Disease, PDF p.196

history: Farmer gave enrofloxacin in drinking water for 5 days for a respiratory problem; last dose this morning. Trader wants to lift the birds tomorrow.
owner_narrative: I finished the enrofloxacin water medicine today. The trader comes tomorrow. Is it okay to sell the birds tomorrow?
question: Can these birds be sold for meat tomorrow?

key_points: SVTG says strict withdrawal periods must be followed after antibiotics, but gives no number for enrofloxacin; do not guess.
Check the product label for the meat withdrawal period counted from the last dose; selling before it ends is not acceptable.
Ask the poultry veterinarian to confirm the withdrawal period before lifting the birds.

history: Ate most of a packet of sugar-free chewing gum labelled 'xylitol' from a handbag about 30 minutes ago. Currently bright and normal.
owner_narrative: My dog ate a packet of sugar-free gum. He seems totally fine and is playing. Can I just keep an eye on him at home?
question: Is xylitol gum dangerous for this dog, and can the owner wait and watch?

key_points: Xylitol is toxic to dogs: it can cause a sudden drop in blood sugar and liver injury.
Do not wait for signs — take the dog to a veterinarian immediately, with the packet.
Do not try home remedies to induce vomiting without veterinary advice.

history: Ate about a cupful of raisins from a festival sweets box roughly two hours ago. Vomited once.
owner_narrative: During Diwali she ate a big handful of kishmish from the sweets box and vomited once. She is a big dog — surely a few raisins can't hurt?
question: How urgent is this?

key_points: Grapes and raisins can cause acute kidney injury in dogs; there is no known safe amount, and size does not protect.
See a veterinarian now for decontamination and kidney monitoring.

history: Free-roaming household dog, never vaccinated against rabies. Bitten by a stray during a fight about three weeks ago. Bit the owner's 9-year-old son on the hand yesterday.
owner_narrative: Our dog has changed — he hides, snaps at us, drools a lot, and can't seem to swallow water. Yesterday he bit my son's hand. We washed it a little. What should we do with the dog?
question: What should be done for the child and the dog?

key_points: Suspected rabies in an unvaccinated dog that has bitten a child: a human medical emergency.
Wash the child's wound with plenty of soap and water for at least 15 minutes and take him to a doctor today for post-exposure anti-rabies vaccination; do not suture or apply turmeric or mud.
Confine the dog safely without handling it; inform the local veterinary/health authority.

source: Not covered by SVTG for dogs; human bite-wound advice follows SVTG 2024 §2.16 Rabies, PDF p.111. Requires veterinarian verification.

history: Indoor cat fed dry food only. Started visiting the litter box repeatedly last evening.
owner_narrative: He keeps going to the litter box and straining but nothing comes out. He cries, licks his private parts and vomited this morning. Maybe he is constipated?
clinical_signs: repeated straining in the litter box with no urine
question: How urgent is this?

acceptable_diagnoses: feline lower urinary tract disease with obstruction
key_points: A male cat straining without producing urine, with vomiting, likely has a urethral obstruction — life-threatening within hours.
Go to a veterinarian immediately; do not treat as constipation at home.

red_flags: male cat unable to pass urine

history: Owner applied a flea spot-on meant for large dogs (contains permethrin) to the cat three hours ago.
owner_narrative: I put my dog's tick-and-flea drops on the cat to save money. Now she is twitching, shaking and drooling. Is the medicine just working?
question: Is this dog flea product safe for the cat?

key_points: Permethrin dog spot-ons are toxic to cats; tremors and twitching mean poisoning, not the medicine working.
Take the cat to a veterinarian immediately; bring the product packaging.
Never use dog flea products on cats.

history: Off food and quiet for one day; feels warm. No vomiting.
owner_narrative: My cat has fever and is very quiet. We have Crocin (paracetamol 500 mg) at home. Can I give her half a tablet tonight?
question: Can the owner give paracetamol to this cat?

key_points: Never give paracetamol (acetaminophen) to cats — even a small amount can be fatal.
Do not give any human painkiller; book a veterinary visit soon to find the cause of the fever.
